title: What memory actually is, and why it is slow
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe a DRAM cell and why it needs refreshing, explain what happens on a read in terms of rows and a row buffer, and account for a 362x difference between two identical loops.

blocks.text: Everything so far has treated main memory as a slow place that caches protect you from. This lesson opens it. The reason memory is slow is not that engineers have failed to make it faster — it is a direct consequence of what a memory cell is made of.

blocks.caption: A DRAM cell
lines: [capacitor]      <- the bit is a charge, or the absence of one
bit line (carries the value in or out)
One transistor and one capacitor per bit. That is why DRAM is dense
and cheap: a static RAM cell, of the kind caches are built from,
needs about six transistors and no capacitor.

blocks.title: The charge leaks, so memory must be rewritten constantly
blocks.text: A capacitor holding a bit is not stable — the charge drains within milliseconds. The memory controller therefore reads and rewrites every row on a schedule, whether or not the program touched it. That is the 'dynamic' in dynamic RAM, and it costs both power and occasional unavailability while a bank is refreshing. A static RAM cell holds its value as long as it is powered, which is one reason caches are fast and also why they are small and expensive.
Reading is destructive, so it happens a row at a time

Sensing the tiny charge on a capacitor drains it. A DRAM read therefore cannot touch one bit: it activates an entire row — thousands of bits — into a set of sense amplifiers called the row buffer, and the row must then be written back. The sequence has names you will see in memory specifications.

rows: Activate the row; its contents land in the row buffer
Select bytes from the row buffer and send them out
Write the row back and prepare for the next activation
A further read from the same row needs only the column step

blocks.title: That last row is the whole performance story
blocks.text: A read from a row that is already open costs one step. A read from a different row costs close-then-open-then-read. This is why memory is not one speed but two, differing by several times, and which one you get is decided entirely by whether consecutive accesses land in the same row.

Build a dependent chain of loads through a 128 MB buffer — far larger than any cache, so every access reaches memory. Run it twice: once with the chain following memory order, once with the same links shuffled into random order. Same buffer, same number of loads, same instructions.

blocks.caption: Measured on an Apple M4
lines: 128 MB buffer, a dependent chain of loads, identical instruction count.
Only the ORDER the chain visits memory in differs.
chain follows memory order :   0.52 ns per access   (0.0104 s total)
chain in random order      : 188.15 ns per access   (3.7629 s total)
/* 0.52 ns is faster than this machine's measured 1.92 ns L1 latency, which
proves those accesses were not actually serialised: the hardware worked
out the addresses ahead of the loads. The random chain gives it nothing
to predict, so each access waits for the one before it. */

blocks.text: Three hundred and sixty-two times, for changing nothing but the order. Two effects compound here: consecutive accesses in memory order stay within the same open row and skip the activation entirely, and their addresses are predictable so the hardware fetches ahead. Random order defeats both, and each access pays the full open-read-close sequence with nothing overlapping it.
Why the parts have the structure they do

rows: Thousands of cells sharing a word line
Reading is destructive, so it happens wholesale
An array of rows with one row buffer
One row open at a time per bank
One bank can open a row while another is being read
More independent paths, so more requests in flight

blocks.text: Every level above the cell exists to work around a limitation of the level below. Banks exist because a single row buffer would serialise everything; channels exist because one path would limit how many requests can be outstanding. The memory controller reorders requests across banks to keep as many rows open and useful as it can — which is one more reason your program's access order matters more than its access count.

blocks.title: This is where the 'random access' in RAM stops being true
blocks.text: The name says any location costs the same as any other. At the level of the interface that is roughly true; at the level of timing it has not been true for decades. A location in an open row is several times cheaper than one in a closed row, and the measurement above shows the difference reaching two orders of magnitude once prefetching is included. Treat 'random access memory' as a statement about addressing, not about cost.

blocks.title: Separate the two effects
steps: Build a 128 MB dependent chain in memory order and time it
Shuffle the chain into random order and time it again
Record the ratio and compare it with the ratio at a 32 KB working set
Explain why the small working set shows almost no difference
Now make a chain that jumps by exactly 8 KB each step, wrapping around
Compare it with the random chain: is a regular large stride as bad as random?
Explain what that comparison tells you about prediction versus row locality
Check whether your machine reports its memory type: system_profiler SPMemoryDataType   or   sudo dmidecode -t memory
blocks.expected: A very large ratio at 128 MB, almost none at 32 KB, and a regular large stride that is faster than random but far slower than sequential. That middle case is the informative one: it separates 'the hardware could predict the address' from 'the access landed in an already-open row', which the sequential and random cases confound together.

cheatsheet: A DRAM cell is one transistor and one capacitor; an SRAM cell is about six transistors
The charge leaks, so every row is refreshed on a schedule — the 'dynamic' in DRAM
Reading drains the cell, so a read activates a whole row into the row buffer
tRCD opens a row, CL reads a column from the row buffer, tRP closes it
A read from an already-open row skips the open and close entirely
Measured: memory-order chain 0.52 ns per access, random-order chain 188.15 ns — 362x
0.52 ns is below the machine's 1.92 ns L1 latency, so those loads were not serialised
Banks let one row open while another is read; channels add independent paths
'Random access memory' describes addressing, not cost

checkpoint.prompt: Why does DRAM need periodic refreshing while SRAM does not?

choices.A: A DRAM bit is a charge on a capacitor that leaks away within milliseconds, while an SRAM cell holds its value as long as it is powered
choices.C: DRAM is further from the processor

checkpoint.explanation: The one-transistor-one-capacitor cell is what makes DRAM dense and cheap, and leakage is the price. SRAM's roughly six transistors hold the value but take far more area.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a DRAM read activate an entire row rather than the bits requested?

choices.B: Sensing the charge on a cell drains it
choices.C: Rows are the unit of refresh
choices.D: The address bus is too narrow to address individual bits

checkpoint.explanation: A read must pull a whole row into sense amplifiers and write it back afterwards. Reading is destructive at the cell level. The row buffer holds the sensed row, and that is also why a second read from the same row is so much cheaper.

checkpoint.prompt: The same 128 MB chain took 0.52 ns per access in memory order and 188.15 ns in random order. What two effects combine to produce that?

choices.A: The random version executed more instructions
choices.C: Consecutive accesses in memory order stay within an already-open row, and their addresses are predictable so the hardware fetches ahead

checkpoint.explanation: Random order defeats both. The instruction counts are identical. Row locality removes the open and close steps, and predictability removes the serialisation — which is why 0.52 ns is below the measured L1 latency.

checkpoint.prompt: Why do memory chips contain multiple banks?

choices.D: A bank has one row buffer

checkpoint.explanation: One row at a time; multiple banks let one row be activated while another is being read. Every level above the cell works around a limit of the level below. One row buffer per bank would serialise every access to a different row.
